utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wanted to raise a preliminary matter. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Yes, Mr. President, as you know the next witness is Colonel Mirko Trivic, and I wanted you to know we had to take your advice on his 92 ter statement. I was able to get it down to 56 pages but -- actually 52 if you take the redacted. So we did get it down to 52. I also noted that we failed to mention to you that he had while testifying initially as a Prosecution witness in the Blagojevic trial, he came back as a Defence expert in the Blagojevic trial and so he is one of our adverse witnesses and -- though we are not asking for a caution to be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No caution to be read to him. You don't think that there is any need for that. Then I think at this moment the Chamber has no reasons to deviate from that proposition. If that would become different, we'll find out. Nothing else, Mr. McCloskey. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trivic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Trivic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by Mr. McCloskey. You find him to your right and Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you tell us your name, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Mirko Trivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And welcome back to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, have you been able to review your testimony from the Popovic case as a Prosecution witness? It was back in May 2007.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I listened to that statement of mine and basically I did understand that. Even six years later I have nothing to add to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions now, would your answers substantially be the same?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The essence of my answers would be the same. Maybe some of the questions -- or, rather, some of the terms used in your questions or in my answers -- maybe, actually, it would have been necessary to say a bit more or to be more specific in my answers in order to give an answer that would be clearer from a substantive point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was your testimony in that case true and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that case and in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer 65 ter 28902 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will not object since the witness is here, but I would leave it to your discretion whether to accept this form of a witness's statement, whether it's in accordance your guidances or not. So I leave it to your discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of objections and using our discretion, the Chamber admits into evidence the testimony -- the transcript of the previous testimony of the witness. Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1463, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 65 ter number was read out, I think, by Mr. McCloskey, and may I take it that that's the reduced version of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, the one that's in e-court, 28902.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And may I read a brief summary. I have explained to the witness about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel Trivic was born in 1949 in the municipality of Bosanska Gradiska, present day Republika Srpska. He is a career army officer. After secondary school, he enrolled in the military academy of the former Yugoslavia in Belgrade and graduated in 1971. From 1971 to 1988 he served in various JNA garrisons in Slovenia. In 1988 he became a teacher of military tactics at the military academy. In 1993 he joined the VRS and was appointed the Chief of Staff of the Guards Brigade, a unit of the Main Staff of the VRS. In 1994 he was appointed commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade of the Drina Corps, taking over from then Colonel Krstic who had been promoted to Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. Trivic was promoted to colonel in January 1995. In early July 1995, he received orders from the Drina Corps to take part in Krivaja 95, the VRS operation concerning the Srebrenica enclave. Colonel Trivic and elements of his brigade took part in the attack on Srebrenica beginning 6 July. By 11 July he and the other VRS officers and units were able to enter Srebrenica town where he met briefly with General Mladic and received orders from him. On 12 July he met with General Krstic in the area of Viogor and received orders to go to Bratunac Brigade headquarters at 2100 hours for a meeting there. He travelled to the Bratunac headquarters that evening and met with other brigade commanders from the operation, as well as General Mladic. General Mladic announced that Zepa would be the next operation and the troops would begin their march to the Zepa area the next day, 13 July. On the morning of 13 July, he was present with his unit in the area of Viogor where General Mladic spoke to the units before their march towards Zepa. Colonel Trivic departed himself toward Zepa on the afternoon of 13 July in the direction of Bratunac, Konjevic Polje, Milici, towards Zepa. And the colonel was wounded in the Zepa operation. And if I could ask some questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, did you receive a preparatory order to get troops ready for the Srebrenica operation in early July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning of July 1995 from the Drina Corps commander. The 2nd Romanija Brigade was given the task to set up a reinforced company equivalent unit and to be prepared for engagement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: -- in an operation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm sorry to interrupt you but I'm going to go briefly to that document and so you'll be able to answer my questions, but we need to be very specific, myself -- or you may be interrupted if you go too far into it. You can always explain your answer but my time is limited. So okay. You've got the order. Let's now go to that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it should be Exhibit 65 ter 04096.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did I give you a copy of this order last night to take a look at?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so if we look at this, we can see that there is a stamp from the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, but can you tell us is this a genuine copy of an order you actually received?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Last night I took a look at this copy. I don't have the original in order to compare. I assume that that is the document. That it's faithful to the original, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you did get an original document like this in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see in the top of it there are "to the commands of" and there are abbreviations for the various brigades. And we have a translation of that in the English. And I am hoping you would clear something up. We see the 2nd Rmtbr. Is that your brigade, the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the 2nd Rmtbr. "2 R" means "Romanija" and then Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we see also the 1st and 5th Plpbr. Does that mean Podrinje Light Infantry Brigades?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I think so. That would be the name of those light infantry brigades, like the Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember, was the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, what -- what city was that associated with?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does Rogatica sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know which unit was where, which unit with what designation, but there were two light Podrinje infantry brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And one was Rogatica and one was Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to spend a lot of time with this preparatory order, but we see that in paragraph 1 it describes the intentions of the Muslim army where it says at the bottom of that paragraph: "At the same time their forces from the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa will act in order to cut the Drina Corps area of responsibility in two and connect the enclaves with the central part of which is held by the Muslims." We couldn't read all of that. Do you see at the bottom of that -- can you read it, but it says: "... connect the enclaves with the central part." Can you read that last sentence for us, if you could make it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could blow it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's that first big paragraph under number 1. When it says: "... connect the ..." --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: You mean, "The last three months..."? Is that what you mean, from there onwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where it says: "Drina Corps area of responsibility in two ..." Just the last two sentences of that second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: In order to have an entire sentence, I would like to start from where it says: "The 5th light Podrinje Brigade ..." And it says: "It is to be expected that the enemy will launch an even heavier offensive of activities in the Kladanj and Olovo area. At the same time, their forces from the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa will act in order to cut the Drina Corps area of responsibility in two and connect the enclaves with the central part of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina which is held by the Muslims." BH is what it says there and that is an abbreviation for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next numbered paragraph it says: "The command of the Drina Corps pursuant to operation Directive number 7 and 7/1 of the main staff ..." Did you receive the Main Staff Directive number 7 and 7/1?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I think I did not receive Directive number 7 because that was written by the Supreme Command. Also, Directive 7/1 which is written by the Main Staff. I think it was sent only to corps level, to the corps command. So the command of the brigade -- the command of any brigade, mine or others, did not receive directives as documents. Rather, what the command regulates on the basis of obligations set in the directives, and they spell them out in operational terms and send tasks to their subordinates on the basis of the task defined and the way in which these tasks will be carried out and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And after this preparatory order, did you receive an actual operations order?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go to 65 ter 04097.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, while we still have the document on our screens, there is something that I seem to remember from the first item in this document that was on our screens. Allow me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: You said something. I'd like --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you need to explain your answer, go ahead. But remember you are not here just to explain. There needs to be question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Just in relation to the question. You said something that is not the essence of the content of the first paragraph of combat documents and orders. In the first paragraph there is an assessment, an estimate of what the enemy is doing. It is not a position that is being stated; namely, that that is exactly what the enemy is going to be doing, that and nothing else. That's the only thing I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would like to offer that document, 04096 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1464, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1464 is it already is evidence. That's how it was announced, isn't it? Oh, no, it's not in evidence yet. It is now hereby admitted into evidence, P1464.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could now go to the next document, the actual operations order, which is 65 ter 04097, and I see it's up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see here that the list of the brigades involved in the order is slightly smaller than the list that went out to the operations group. Is this deliberate?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Please, I don't want to give any explanations but I would like to say why I think that is the case in my view. It was sent to all the units of the Drina Corps, the preparatory order, so that they would have some of their forces on the ready for some planned activity in the forthcoming period. After consultations, and obviously the assessment that was made by the corps command, regarding the necessities involved in carrying out that attack, they came to the position that it was only necessary that this was to be sent only to these units. And then further on, this order for active operations was sent to this unit only on the basis of estimated needs in relation to what all the brigades were expecting. They expected that part of their forces would be engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And does this -- is this an order you actually received yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: There is no reason for me to express any doubts, and I think that that was the order received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I gave you a copy of that last night to review as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now we see from the beginning of this order, and I don't want to read it all out, but in paragraph 1 the order is describing that the enemy, the Muslim army, has carried out attacks with a limited objectives against the Drina Corps units. And that in the coming period they expect other attacks. And as we read it, by the 28th Division, from the enclave of Srebrenica and Zepa in order to cut the Drina Corps area in two and connect the enclaves with the central part of the territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. It goes on then to describe in the next big paragraph that the Muslim forces from the enclave of Zepa and Srebrenica have been particularly active, that they were sabotage groups that were attacking and burning unprotected villages, killing civilians, and small isolated units around the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica. And that they are trying especially hard to link up the enclaves and open a corridor to Kladanj. Then it describes what the various units of the 28th Division are and it describes information on them which I -- which I won't go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the page 3 in the English and it's paragraph 2 in the B/C/S. Numbered paragraph 2. It may be the third page of the B/C/S as well. It should be -- yes, that's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And looking at this numbered paragraph 2, we again see this reference that now: "The command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to operations Directive 7 and 7/1 of the Main Staff ..." Now, can you tell us, General [sic], what was the objective of this operation that we are looking at, Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for promoting me. I'm a colonel, not a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps command formulated the task based on these directives as I have said in the answer to your first question, and this was all based on the preparatory order. The goal was to use the available forces for an offensive, and it was defined as an order for active combat activities. Further, the objective was to separate the enclaves Zepa and Srebrenica in the depth of the territory, and this is how they set out to accomplish this objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Aside from splitting the two enclaves, was there another objective?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Narrowing. Narrowing them down by separating them, by splitting the enclaves. The physical process was actually squeezing the units and narrowing the area that they had under their control, the enemy forces. The area from which they conducted activities in various forms. They were not planned offensive activities of the entire 28th Division but rather they used various brigades in various sectors and some favorable positions to carry out small attacks, sabotage activities --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: -- minor incursions and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can actually see here in the last sentence of paragraph 2: "In order to split the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and to reduce them to their urban areas." So this reduction you are talking about is to reduce the size of the enclave to that urban area of Srebrenica and that urban area of Zepa, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that if we are to strictly interpret this, then this wouldn't cover Zepa because Zepa was really not a town. It was a village, a small village. So reducing this to the area that belonged to Srebrenica municipality, if I may be a bit more clear, this was to be within the observation points of the United Nations so that they wouldn't be leaving that area. This was to be the area that was to be the town of Srebrenica from 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't argue with you, Colonel, but we see here very clearly written: "In order to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and to reduce them to their urban area ..." Urban does not include the vast and very wooded and rural municipality of Srebrenica, does it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that this term "urban" was inappropriately used here, awkwardly used here, but let us go back to how it functioned in 1995. The enclave of Srebrenica and the enclave of Zepa. In 1993 both enclaves were defined and those were their defined areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go down under paragraph 4 which you should be able to see. And under -- it's basically the second paragraph under paragraph 4, and it gives us a title: "Objective." And it says: "By a surprise attack to separate and reduce in size the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, to improve the tactical positions of the forces in the depth of the area, and to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." So one of the other objectives that you didn't mention was to create the conditions for the actual elimination of the enclaves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I haven't mentioned that. It is true. It's not mentioned in item 2, in paragraph 2 -- or, rather, in paragraph 2 they speak of the task and then under 4, where they discuss objective, they say "separate and reduce and create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." I wish to comment on this given that you deepened further your question. The separation of the enclaves and reduction to the area as it was defined in the resolutions establishing them is that improve the tactical position of the units of the Drina Corps and created conditions for activities which, in this order, order for activities, were not envisioned. Nobody was issued the task of eliminating the enclaves. Simply by successfully implementing this order one would create conditions that in some other situation, having assessed the enemy forces positions and so on, would enable forces to perhaps continue with another task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, we are not here to hear the exegesis of the documents. If you have any facts you could mention which support your interpretation of the document, we'd like to hear that and otherwise the Chamber will interpret the documentary evidence in the totality of the evidence. Are there any facts known to you which support your interpretation which seems to be slightly not fully consistent with the language of the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for guiding me in giving my answers. This order, Mr. President, is the order for active combat activities. In item 4, they define the objective of those activities. And the end objective was to carry out that assignment, to separate the enclaves, and by achieving that objective they simply added that that would create the conditions for eliminating the enclaves. I did not put in any new elements in giving my interpretation of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may not have fully understood my guidance. Next question, please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, did something come up in the next few days that changed this limited attack order and actually include a further objective that you became aware of?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely so. When they began activities pursuant to this order, conditions were created for changing the objectives and the directions of the attack. In two days before they entered into Srebrenica, they amended the tasks given to battalions and units which participated in the offensive pursuant to this order, and it was only on the 11th based on the conditions that were created and pursuant to the permission to enter the enclave, that they entered the enclave and the enclave ceased to exist. However, the conditions were not created solely by the combat activities of two or three battalions participating pursuant to this order but also by the enemy who contributed to these conditions by deserting the positions and opening up the passage into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to 65 ter 04024. This is a 9 July document that -- oh, and I would like to - I'm sorry, Your Honour - offer that previous 04097 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is supposed to remain seated. Mr. Mladic, remain seated, as I said before. Sit down. Mr. Lukic, any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1465, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1465 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, yes, if we could have 65 ter 04024 on the -- there it is in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, we can see that this is not to any brigades. In fact, it's to the president of the Republika Srpska and the Drina Corps forward command post, General Gvero and Krstic personally from General Tolimir. And we see that what Tolimir says in this paragraph beginning: "The president of Republika Srpska has been informed of successful combat operations around Srebrenica by units of the Drina Corps and that they have achieved results which enable them to occupy the very town of Srebrenica." Now, does this change anything? Does this have anything to do with what you are talking about? As we go on and read it, it basically gives the go ahead to go into Srebrenica but abide by the Geneva Conventions about property and civilians. How does this fit into your previous answers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: This is a logical continuation of the events which took place between the 6th and the 9th, but mostly on the 9th. A sequence of steps which represent a textbook example of how command and reporting functions through the units of the Drina Corps to the Main Staff and up to the Supreme Commander, where they report on the activities of some units. I suppose that assistant commander General Tolimir informed about the results of the activities. On the 9th of July, he reported to the president of the republic. Well, to the Supreme Commander but first and foremost to the minister of defence, and then based on the feedback pursuant to that report, he was sending information to the forward command post of the Drina Corps by send -- but also sent a similar document for information of the president of the republic. So Tolimir sent this document to the Drina Corps forward command post informing that the approval was given and making an assessment that the access to Srebrenica was open by eliminating the enclave, that there was no major opposition, the permission to enter was given. And there is also a caution given about the civilians, civilian population and forces that are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just ask for one clarification, Mr. Trivic. You said: "Well, he reported to the president of the --" it's -- in the transcript it is not correct. "Well, to the Supreme Command, but first and foremost to the minister of defence." Please, can you help me, to show where I can find that in the document, that he reported to the minister of defence? Where can I find it in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to reply to the question posed by Mr. McCloskey; namely, whether this document reflects what I said earlier about the task and the conditions for eliminating the enclaves. I tried to reply by trying to explain about who was informed on the 9th about the results achieved and conditions created, who was informed by the staff, and that this was the logical path of reporting. They had to report that the Drina Corps was achieving results which created conditions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as a result of which permission was given to enter Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to stop you here. Please help me, was this letter signed by Mr. Tolimir sent to the minister of defence -- to the Ministry of Defence or was it -- was this information given by other means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will try to clarify. This is a cable that was sent on the 9th. It was marked "very urgent." It was sent to two locations. This cable was sent to two locations: To the president of republic for his information and to the forward command post of the Drina Corps as the document containing a position that had to be implemented, that had to be carried out. It was sent for the information only to the president of the republic to inform him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is well understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is well understood. Please help me to understand why you said it was sent to the Ministry of Defence. Where can I find it? I am only interested in this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't find it in this document. However, the minister of defence is a specialised professional person via whom documents are transmitted to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I would offer this 04024 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1466, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I want to take you briefly to 11 July where we know that the VRS, General Mladic, and others, were able to go into Srebrenica town. And do you recall seeing yourself on video greeting General Mladic in Srebrenica town on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we have all seen that. I don't think we need to spend the time to go through that. And it's clearly identified in the stills book. Did you -- do you recall hearing General Mladic on the radio that day talking about air strikes?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your question was on the radio. It wasn't on the radio, it was in the communications system that existed between the units taking part in this operation. It was on the radio communications system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you hear General Mladic say?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: That taking advantage of his presence at the forward command post of the Drina Corps, General Mladic sent out a circular memo to all units taking part in this operation saying that the NATO air strikes were expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, nodding yes or no to whomever is not permitted. That could be understood as comments on testimony given, so you should refrain from doing these kind of things. And you know what the consequences are if you continue. I thought, Mr. Lukic, that Mr. Mladic was seeking a consultation at a moment ago, but perhaps if that could wait for five minutes then you have an opportunity to do it during the break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did General Mladic say this before any air strikes had occurred?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I have said, he sent out a circular memo to all commanders, all units taking part in these activities, warning them that there was an estimate that there could be a NATO air strikes on the forces in that area. So he announced that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you're going to get us in trouble. That was a very simple question and required a simple answer. You can always explain but remember our time, as is the Defence's, is limited. Okay. So now in your statement we know that the night of the 11th you go back to your command post where you were staying at Jasenova and that on the 12th of July you were involved in a sweep operation, and that General Krstic tells you to go to a meeting on the evening of the 12th of July at the Bratunac headquarters; is that correct, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the activities in the course of that day. I think in one of the earlier answers to your questions concerning the sweeping operation, I asked that the term "sweep operation" for the 12th not be used because on the 12th it was a continuation of the offensive activities which ended up in chasing, chasing enemy forces. That's what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. And did you make -- did you have a wartime diary where you filled out some events and thoughts as you went along at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we now go to 65 ter 25860. It should be page 25 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, I'm just jumping to the 12 July entry. We see that's the front of your little ringed binder on the left. And if we could go to page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be 25 in both languages. And if we could blow those up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't want to spend time on this one. I just wanted to show that we've written -- excuse me, you've written 0900 hours, 12 July, and some notes there that we can read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to the next page in both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And are we still on 12 July here, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Could you put back the previous page, please, so I can see the page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go back in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Number 12. And the second page -- I mean, I just want to confirm what I said. It's not a sweep operation. It's just that the attack should be continued along certain axes. Now we can move onto the other page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a few minutes on this diary but I see it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said a few minutes on this diary. And is that all?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. It's almost all but it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if it's not all, then we'll take the break first. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break and will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to go on to the next page in the -- in the diary. And then now -- as we are still on the 12th, so let's go to the next page. Now -- all right. Now here is a reference that you've scratched down that the brigade commanders are to come to the Drina Corps IKM in Bratunac by 2100 hours via Srebrenica and Potocari. And did you actually go that evening at 2100 hours to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then you note that General Mladic came at 2200 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He arrived at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters at 2200 hours?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see here that it says in the English: "By 0800 hours tomorrow, General Kostic must prepare a decision ..." Which general should that be?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And there is also a note -- we see that -- who ordered General Krstic to prepare a decision to go to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And there is a note here that Vinko Pandurevic and I warned him that the soldiers should rest. And you and now Pandurevic warned who that the soldiers should rest?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Here in my text it says "made aware of," regardless of the fact that Vinko Pandurevic and I made him aware of. So it wasn't "upgrozali," [phoen] it was "upoznali" [phoen]. It was misread. So although he was made aware of that, he issues an order that General Krstic carry out the decision to free Zepa the next day and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could the transcription be verified for this page. We have now a second where the witness comments on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Krstic, Kostic, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We will get the revision to look at that. That's important, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this document 65 ter 25860. There is just a section. It's in the English so it's not too long, and I think it should all go in. I think there is -- it would assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've looked at a few pages. I see in e-court it's a 76-page document, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me then -- I didn't think we had that many in English. We're perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, sometimes perhaps they are short, but I see at least 76 -- 67 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, 76 pages, I apologise, in e-court. I suggest the following. That it will be marked for identification. That you do two things: First of all to further select the portions you need or explain why we need the whole of the document in evidence; and second, that you verify the transcription of the pages you used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was not aware that it was that long. We'll only -- we'll get together, but I think it's just July we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do not object to the portions used during the trial since it's obvious that things have to be explained, but we would object to anything that's not used today in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, unless we could foresee that it will be used soon and what pages will be used, then perhaps. But as matters stand now, the document will be MFI'd. Mr. Registrar, the document now still 76 pages would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1467, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. And when do we hear from you, Mr. McCloskey? Is it within the next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tomorrow. All I will want is the Srebrenica operation notes and that will be very limited, and they actually go along with his testimony and I think will be valuable for the Trial Chamber and it won't be anywhere near 76 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what I see apparently is that the English is consistent with the original because the original is also 76 pages. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just lastly, Colonel, and related to you and Colonel Pandurevic making General Mladic aware that the soldiers needed rest, I want to go to something you said in your Popovic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's P1463, e-court 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'll read it slowly in English because we don't have a Serbian for you. But it's on that same topic where you and Colonel Pandurevic are talking with Mladic that evening about the men needing rest, and I think you -- he then agrees to come to Viogor the next morning to give them a talk which is in your statement. I won't go over that. But I want to just read you something, and you may remember when Mr. Thayer asked you this as you were explaining the question, he goes, this is Mr. Thayer's question to you: "Well, sir, in response to being overruled, did you or Colonel Pandurevic make any suggestions to Generals Krstic and Mladic?" And your answer was: "We were not out-voted. It's not right to put it that way. It is the unquestionable right of the commander to make decisions. We tried to suggest that this part of the troops that had been involved in the operations thus far..." and that they take a rest. Can you explain to us what you meant when you say that it is the unquestionable right of the commander to make the decisions, suggesting it's not to a vote? What -- is that a military principle you can explain briefly to us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that this Court, since it has been dealing with the question of warfare for so long and has been investigating what happened from different angles but is primarily dealing with combat operations, military matters, and so on, it must have come to the conclusion that I have already referred to. There is no voting and out-voting. It wasn't a debate. It is the commander's right to say, "All right. All of that is well and fine what you said, but ..." I think that in one of my statements in one of the cases, I did say that -- explaining the reasons why soldiers needed some rest, I said it's not about the commander accepting or not accepting something. A motive also had to be found for staying on under such conditions, and then when such a decision is made which is undeniably the right of the commander who said that this should be taken advantage of, this moment of success, that this morale should be carried through and the second enclave should be taken care of as well. Then he insisted that he come and state that personally because when he personally speaks to the soldiers, then they can endure in spite of these problems that cropped up over those 15 days or so that they spent in the field in different conditions without anything comfortable about it and so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, you might not have understood the question. What Mr. McCloskey would like to know is whether it is a military rule that if the higher in command decides, even if that is not in line what was advised to him by his subordinate officers, that only the decision of the commander is what counts. Is that -- I think that is what Mr. McCloskey wanted to know. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my position, but both for Mr. McCloskey and you, you do oversimplify relations within a command. There is no discussion there. I mean, a subordinate can say: "Sorry, I think that we should wait, that we should not set out." But it's for the commander to say: "All right. We have to complete this mission as soon as possible, and as soon as this is over then we can get some rest." But there is no discussion there as far as combat operations are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is clear. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In fact, it was my last question. No, no, no, Mr. McCloskey is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You got it just right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Trivic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trivic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just unpack, if you will. Good day, Mr. Trivic.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this stage of the Tribunal, our time is rather limited as you've seen when you were answering the Prosecutor's questions, and we have quite a few things to deal with with you, so please let us be as specific as possible so that we can cover as much material as possible in terms of everything that we have prepared because we would like to take advantage of your experience and your knowledge of things as they happened. Also, we have to bear in mind the fact that our questions and answers should not overlap because we speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1464. That is what I would like to start with today. It was used by the Prosecutor as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll see the document in a moment. You gave your comments today with regard to this document, and this is what I'd like to ask you. This preparatory order of the 2nd of July, 1995, does it deal with the enemy's offensive actions primarily in the spring of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of the content of the first paragraph, one may infer that that the estimate was -- not only estimate but also there is an analysis of what happened in the spring of 1995 in that area. And there is a reference to operations that were carried out in villages around the enclaves and also the deployment of defence positions of brigades that did hold position vis-a-vis these enclaves. One may conclude that this is an analysis on the basis of which this order was written, including the tasks involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the ground, did you see and feel these offensive activities of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to say that the brigade that I commanded, that I headed, did not hold positions vis-a-vis the enclaves but in other areas towards Kladanj, Olovo. There weren't any major operations but there were some attempts to break through the positions that were held by my brigade, but I did not feel that there were incursions out of the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time were you informed in the field that attempts were being made to cut Republika Srpska into two and to link up the enclaves with the rest of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The areas that are referred to as areas where the enemy is carrying out offensive operations are areas that are covered by the 2nd Krajina Corps, the Sarajevo Corps, the Drina Corps, the Eastern Bosnian Corps. Those are the corps of the Army of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, there is a reference to a large part of the territory of Republika Srpska that the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina are attacking, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is practically all of Republika Srpska that was covered by these corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your units, did they take part in the defence from these attacks and were you helping the Zvornik Brigade in that way?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All units that this order that is before us pertains to, P1464 is how we have marked it, they are part of the Drina Corps, all of them, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This order was not sent to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska; is that correct? Can you see that from the document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: This preparatory order?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was not supposed to be sent. Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't supposed to be sent. It is correct that it was not necessary to send it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly take a look at 1D976 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you can actually see it, I'll say that this is a document of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 17th of June, 1995. And it is a document that is entitled: "Preparations for Offensive Combat Operations Order." And in paragraph 1 it says that the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Corps, Sulejman Budakovic, is issuing the order as follows: "Execute all preparations in the command of the 28th land army division to execute offensive combat operations with a view to liberating the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina overextending the AS and --" it says "AS" or "KS" here, "inflicting losses, co-ordinate the action with the BH Army forces carrying out operations in the SS area of Sarajevo." At that time were you aware that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was attempting to take control of the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. By carrying out tasks and by conducting individual operations in certain areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina to take hold of that particular area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but especially to split apart the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you had no contact with the enclaves, the brigade under your command. However, did you have any intelligence to the effect that the units of the 28th Division from Srebrenica and Zepa carried out attacks from the safe havens towards the depth of the territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had intelligence on the number of forces first and foremost in the territory in the area of the Drina Corps and such information reached the command of the brigade on a daily basis. In addition to that, in addition to the intelligence, I also received information about the losses and things that were taking place in certain villages, in positions, and in certain sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that not only the villages on the demarcation line were attacked but also the villages in the depth of the territory of Republika Srpska, did you receive information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And one of the most vivid pieces of information that I will never forget, I think it involved the village of Visnjica, if I still remember correctly, there was a massacre that took place there against the residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Visnjica, that attack of the 28th Division against the village, was that the pretext for Krivaja 95 operation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the straw that broke the camel's back that prompted the corps command to start implementing the objectives from the Directive 7/1 by conducting active operations in their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will get to the directive soon. I would like to ask you now something about end of June, early July, of 1995 and the Krivaja operation. So first you came to Bratunac to the command of the Drina Corps when you reached that area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: You mean the Bratunac Brigade? Are you referring to the forward command post of the Drina Corps that was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, you just tell us where you went on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, I went -- I reported to the command, to the command post of the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac, but I did not report to the commander of the brigade; rather, I reported to General Krstic who was the commander of the operation and used that command post as the command post for that particular operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this is where you were -- where you received your orders, your tasks, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, the last defining of the tasks took place there. As for the implementation of the tasks in the area, that took place near an observation post near Pribecevci [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you were receiving your tasks in Bratunac and also as the details were worked out in Pribicevac, is it true that you did not see anybody from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: That is right. I did not see them there. None of them were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Krivaja 95 operation was the operation of the Drina Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps planned out this operation and carried it out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Both operations, the one on Srebrenica and on Zepa, both of these two actions were those of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The competence for carrying out these actions, operations, was within the command of the Drina Corps which carried it out together with its unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the primary objective was to split, to separate the enclaves and that the additional objective once the conditions were created, as we could see earlier, further to the question put by Mr. McCloskey, so the -- following that the additional objective was the demilitarisation of the enclaves as it had been agreed back in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was answering one of Mr. McCloskey's questions, I explained my position regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you something now about the Muslim forces in Srebrenica. So let us first take a look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before we do that, I would like to offer this document that is on our screens to be admitted. [In English] I would tender this document on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 1D976, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D286, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D286 [Realtime transcript read in error "P286"] is admitted into evidence. I think I said D286 and that's -- yes, D286 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Now we should see on the screens 65 ter 18150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number. It's not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. 18150, 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the document of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, command of the 28th Division in Srebrenica, dated 6th June, 1995. This is the document which analyses the manpower per combat arms. It was sent to the command of the 2nd Corps in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the second page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And here you will see the segment that reads "ARJ PVO." Can you tell us what this acronym stands for?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: It stands for artillery and rocket units of the anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will see that this document lists commanders of various units. So under number 4, 5, 7, 11, 12, 16, 17, 20, 24, 25, you can see that it says PAT-20/1. What does that stand for, PAT-20/1?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: It stands for anti-aircraft gun, 21-millimetre calibre with one barrel. So the calibre is 20 [as interpreted] millimetres and it is an anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then under number 4, you can see rocket S-2M. What is S-2M?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: That is a mobile anti-aircraft rocket carried by individuals and its name is Strela 2M for anti-aircraft combat. It is used to fire at the departing aircraft because it follows the fumes, the exhaust fumes of the aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under number 6, 13, 18, 21, we can see commanders of units which have that weapon in their arsenal.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you come under fire from this weapon during the activities around Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I think that I did in the Slapovici sector on the second day, which is to say on the 10th of July, in the early stage of the continuation of the attack following the change of the original direction. So once the conditions were created, my units came under fire from this weapon. So my units were under fire from these weapons, these anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying. I did ask about these anti-aircraft guns. Obviously I didn't think that they were firing anti-aircraft rockets at you. Now that you are mentioning the 10th, is it true that on that day the forces of the 28th Division commenced the counter-attack and pushed back the Serbian forces back to their initial positions?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: In some areas, yes. In the areas where I was, probably owing partially to my influence as well given that I was deployed with the units carrying out the incursion against those positions, our -- in those areas where I was, we were somewhat former [as interpreted], and they didn't manage to push us back. However, I managed to get back a tank which had been resubordinated to our neighbour on the right side, and owing to the fire from that tank, those positions were neutralised and my forces were not moved from their original positions, and then we carried on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that owing to the existence of these weapons within the enclave, it wasn't safe to fly above Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That certainly contributed to their no-being-safe area for flights above Srebrenica, these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Srebrenica and Zepa were five to six times more numerous than the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska which were carrying out the attack.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps even more than that. I'm saying this without a trace of exaggeration or disparaging. When one analyses the order and the forces that were involved in active operations in order to split the enclaves, then the ratio is even greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was much easier to defend Srebrenica and Zepa and that area than to attack it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, given the configuration of the terrain and the long-term fortifications that had been put in place there. It was much easier to be in defence there, to defend the area than to attack it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that your impression as someone who took part in those operations that the withdrawal of the members of the 28th Division from the enclaves of Srebrenica was not only of a military but also of a political nature?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with what you said. And I hope there will be other opportunities for me to expand on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We will get to that point as well. Now let me ask you something about the relations between the Army of Republika Srpska and the UNPROFOR forces. Earlier on you testified and I would ask you to explain to us whether you were aware of the plans of some of UNPROFOR officers to use helicopters for flying above Srebrenica in order to provoke fire for which the Serbs would be blamed. The Serbs would be blamed for knocking down the helicopters which in turn would be punished by air strikes against the forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not at that time, but later on, while working in various cases and in my various roles at the Tribunal, I managed to see certain documents which refer to that and confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this was proposed by General Smith to the command in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Based on his statement given in 1996, there is a part of that statement that confirms that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when the operation was being carried out, did you have the impression and was that the prevalent opinion within the VRS that by then UNPROFOR had openly sided with the other warring party?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: That was discussed very often, and in July, I could conclude myself that there were such cases, especially where my unit was involved. It was in the area of Zepa when I was being attacked. There were APCs, sandbags at UN points, and that was confirmed. Until then, we were told about that from other areas. It was intelligence from other areas. But then I saw it for myself. That was confirmation that that's exactly the way it was, that the United Nations was being used for protecting the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Despite that, what kind of orders did you receive? How were you supposed to behave towards members of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The orders we received verbally and in writing and in all contacts were that we should no behave improperly and that we should not thereby imperil our positions and the legitimacy of the VRS for carrying out combat operations in accordance with the rules of warfare, and that is how we did behave. There are many confirmations of that, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Like the Prosecutor today when we started, I'm going to ask for a clarification of a term so that I do not use it wrongly. Was this an action, "akcija," or operation, "operacija," of the VRS as far as Srebrenica was concerned?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to the rules for combat documents and for the works of -- for the work of commands and staffs, offensive activity is active combat, and this was not an operation carried out at corps level as a whole. But since the corps command led this - how do I put this? - in its name it had to include the word "operacija," operation, the code-name was Krivaja 95. But basically this was an operation of trying to take care of positions, et cetera, and not all units were involved in carrying out these active operations. The level of the units involved was below the brigade level. So it wasn't even a brigade level. It was battalion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat something, this very last part of your answer because it was not recorded. The last thing that was recorded was: "So it wasn't even brigade level."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The order for active operations in the part where tasks are being issued to individual units, one can see that there aren't even units at infantry brigade level. All of them are lower-ranking. So it wasn't even an operation at brigade level. Quite simply, it was an operation that was called an "action," that is, active combat. I don't know English, so I don't know whether this last part has been interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were told that UNPROFOR and its members were not the target of the actions of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly there was that kind of cautioning that was effected, that certainly it wasn't the forces of the UN, UNPROFOR, that were the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your soldiers from the units that you commanded, did they obey these instructions?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Well, I insisted that they obey this. Of course, I could not see everything, but there weren't any reports to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 9th of July, 1995. That's what I'd like to move on to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll need document number 65 ter 04024. That's what we'd like to have in e-court. I think that we used it today. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's now P1466.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] P1464 [as interpreted], could we now have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any intentions to tender the document which is on our screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 18150 receives number D287, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D287 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were asked about this document today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I wrote this down somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this document, who is it that is agreeing to the entering into enclaves? Because page 18, line 1, of today's LiveNote is unclear. It says: "[In English] The permission to enter was given." "The permission to enter was given." [Interpretation] That is how it was recorded in the transcript. Sorry, does this document show --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: This document shows in paragraph 2 that it says: "The president of the republic is satisfied with the results of combat operations around Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation of operations for the take-over of Srebrenica, disarming of Muslim terrorist gangs, and complete demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave." So this is General Tolimir. He sent this. He informed the forward command post of the Drina Corps. He said that the president of Republika Srpska was satisfied and that they could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we'd need document 1D973.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before I move onto this document, I'd just like to ask you something that my learned friend Mr. McCloskey dealt with on page 5 today. In line 7, this is what he said. I'll start reading this out in English so that you could get the right interpretation. This is a summary of your statement. This is what it says: "[In English] By 11 July, the other VRS officers and units were able to enter Srebrenica town where he met briefly with General Mladic and received orders from him ..." [Interpretation] The order that you received was the direction of the Bratunac, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember. However, this part, "other officers could enter," that confused me a bit. General Mladic did utter those words, "ahead Bratunac," that was not the order -- this was not issued as an order and I did not understand that to be an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it carried out all?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No, not on my part, and I think that other commanders did not take it that way either, did not carry this out as an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you were referring to the summary of the evidence of the witness which is not evidence, so there is no need to correct that. If there is anything in the evidence which needs correction, then please do so, but there is no need to seek further comment on the summary. It's just -- if you think that the summary is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My learned friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. There -- in the previous testimony he does actually state what orders he received from Mladic at the time and that, of course, would be the appropriate thing to be referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you can examine the witness on that but not by putting to him the summary read by Mr. McCloskey. But, of course, if the summary accurately reflects what he said then, and if you want to challenge that, then you should --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the microphone be switched off for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is not receiving -- oh, okay. It's okay now. He wasn't receiving translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently it has been resolved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I finished with this clarification. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D973 is the document that we have before us. This is a document from the 9th of July. This fits into what we were discussing about relations with UNPROFOR. This is an interim combat report. Major-General Radislav Krstic. Paragraph 4, we see it's entitled "Conduct of UNPROFOR forces." It says: "UNPROFOR forces at the check-points in Slapovici village and Bucje village surrendered fully to our forces with all their weapons and equipment and asked for our protection. Ten (10) UNPROFOR soldiers from the UNPROFOR check-point in the village of Bucje have been sent to and accommodated in Milici, while five soldiers from the check-point in Slapovici have been accommodated in Bratunac. UNPROFOR forces from the base in Potocari village did not intervene at the check-points or attack our forces." Do you know about these things? Do you know that this happened when UNPROFOR soldiers asked the VRS for their help and crossed over to their side?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, your unit, come across these UNPROFOR soldiers in the village of Slapovici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That part of the village of Slapovici that was like a refugee camp for the Muslim population. A crew of an APC encountered me or I encountered them in this group that was with me. They came out and they surrendered. I mean surrendered in the sense of walking out of the APC with their hands up, and they asked to be taken out of this area of combat activity and that was indeed done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This interim combat report in part speaks about that, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have more on this topic but I think it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, it is indeed time for a break. Could I invite the parties, the issue we had a few minutes ago about was there an order, was that what the witness testified in the previous case, did he understand it to be an order, was it executed by the others, yes, but not as an order, that was all rather vague and all rather ambiguous. It would assist me, perhaps my colleagues as well, to have those matters clarified. But then not on the basis of the summary but then on the basis of the evidence. The witness may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I may be able to clear that up with a brief explanation that my guess is my colleague would agree with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then coffee or tea. Use the next break to see whether you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was thinking of directing it to the Trial Chamber to see if that would help put it in context and that might help us guide our coffee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To say that it's entirely clear to me, Mr. McCloskey, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can clarify some of the issues for you. That's one of the problems with only taking an hour. These issues have been flushed out in greater detail, and I think if I explained it in two minutes my colleague would probably agree with me and it may help direct us to any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Give it a try during the break in the presence of Mr. Lukic, and then if he does agree then you'll certainly agree that you'll address the Chamber in that way, and then we'll hear that this is what Mr. Lukic agrees to, and it may be of guidance for us for further questions. We take a break and we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me, before that, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If you have -- well, there is no problem, I take it, if the witness would hear it, because it's apparently something you agree upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well -- and the witness may have his views as well. But one thing we did agree upon that we suggest is there is a very brief video segment where Colonel Trivic meets General Mladic and the comments "go to Bratunac" are mentioned which has started this. I was going to play it. But you just saw this with the last witness whose name I won't mention. But for this particular issue, it helps to originate it with that -- with that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clearly on my mind. That gives the factual basis for whatever interpretation you may have on whether these are orders or not orders or, of course, it doesn't say anything about whether they were executed yes or no. But that is clear, you say, for both, that is the factual basis for that portion of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It -- yes. And, Mr. President, just so you understand, it's from this video that the -- the witness will say that the orders to go towards Bratunac, that they were able to talk the general out of that and he was to security the heights. And that is what is in his transcript that is in evidence on page 28 of e-court. But to get to that, and that was the order I was referring to in the summary, but to get to that we do -- I -- hopefully it won't confuse the issues to see the -- to see the you actual videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the videotape where there is a conversation in the streets and that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the persons are identified. We have them on the stills. So the Chamber is sufficiently aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
